scope.start: 87b: R. Asi of Neharbil on blood plasma, R. Yirmeya of Difti, and the Tosefta on a corpse's liquids (88a opens mid-exchange with the mishna of Tevul Yom)
scope.end: 88b: Rava's aggada on Abraham's "dust and ashes" (the second Rava statement continues on 89a)

sections.title: Blood Plasma: Machshir, Karet, and Tumat Ohel
sections.gist: R. Asi and R. Yirmeya treat the clear serum of blood as blood for rendering food susceptible, while *karet* and corpse-impurity require a full measure of actual blood.

bullets.text: R. Asi of Neharbil: Rav Yehuda's ruling refers to blood plasma — if it has a reddish hue from the blood it has the status of blood and renders food susceptible to impurity.

Rashi: when blood is left to settle, the denser matter collects toward the center and the clearer, watery portion pools at the edges; even that separated serum still counts as blood for *hechsher zera'im*.
R. Yirmeya of Difti: consuming this plasma is punishable by *karet*, as with blood, provided there is at least a *kezayit* of actual blood.

Tosafot applies R. Yirmeya's qualification both to blood mixed with water and to the separated water-component of blood: either way the *kezayit* is measured from the actual blood, not from the mixture as a whole.
Baraita: plasma issuing from a corpse that has a reddish hue imparts impurity in a tent, provided there is at least a quarter-*log* of actual blood.
The upshot is an intermediate status for the serum: connected enough to blood to render food susceptible, yet not itself enough to carry *karet* or *tumat ohel* without the measure of red blood.
Tosefta (*Oholot* 4:5): all liquids that issue from a corpse — teardrops, breastmilk — are pure, except for its blood; and any of its liquids bearing a reddish hue of blood impart impurity in a tent.

The passage is introduced with the language of "we learned" even though it is found in the Tosefta and not in a Mishnah; R. Shimshon notes that the manuscripts read so, and Tosafot acknowledges that the Gemara sometimes uses the term imprecisely.

sections.title: Are a Corpse's Liquids Really Pure?
sections.gist: A mishna about the liquids of impure persons seems to contradict the Tosefta, and the Gemara resolves it by reading "major sources" as a *zav*, then explains why a *zav* was decreed upon and a corpse was not.

children.title: The Mishna of Tevul Yom: Liquids That Issue and Liquids Touched
children.gist: For one who immersed that day, the liquids that leave his body are like liquids he touches — and neither imparts impurity.

bullets.text: Mishna (*Tevul Yom* 2:1): liquids that issue from one who immersed that day have the same status as liquids that he touches.
And both these and those do not impart ritual impurity.

A *tevul yom* is on the level of a *sheni*; ordinarily a *sheni* touching liquid raises the liquid to *rishon*, a stringency unique to liquids, but since he is already on his way out of impurity the Sages did not apply it to him.
The same stringency underlies drying one's hands after *netilat yadayim*: hands are treated as a *sheni*, so water left on them becomes a *rishon* and would recontaminate the bread.

children.title: All Other Sources, and the Exception of an Av HaTumah Liquid
children.gist: For every other source of impurity the liquids that issue are first-degree impure, unless the liquid is itself a primary source of impurity.

bullets.text: For all other sources of impurity, minor or major, liquids that issue from them have the same status as liquids that touch them, and both are first-degree impure, since they touched a primary source upon exiting.
The exception: a liquid that is itself a primary source of ritual impurity.

Those are the liquids of a *zav*, *zavah* and *niddah* — spit, urine and semen — derived from "*vechi yarok hazav*", fluids that collect in the body before being expelled; their blood, tears and sweat are impure only as a *rishon*.

The seven liquids are *yayin*, *devash*, *shemen*, *chalav*, *tal*, *dam* and *mayim* (*yad shachat dam*). That dew is listed separately shows "water" is a restricted category, so tears and urine are not among the seven, and Tosafot suggests they may not be biblically susceptible at all.

children.title: Resolution: "Major Sources" Means a Zav, Not a Corpse
children.gist: The contradiction dissolves once "minor" is read as a creeping animal and "major" as a *zav*, leaving a corpse's non-blood liquids pure.

bullets.text: The Gemara asks what "minor sources" and "major sources" mean: if minor means a creeping animal or a *zav* and major means a corpse, the mishna would teach that all a corpse's liquids are impure, against the baraita.

Answer: "minor" refers to a creeping animal — e.g. urine found inside its body, which is not impure — and "major" refers to a *zav*, all of whose liquids are impure. A corpse's liquids remain pure, with the exception of blood.

children.title: Why the Sages Decreed for a Zav but Not for a Corpse
children.gist: People do not instinctively keep away from a *zav*, so his liquids were included by rabbinic decree; from a corpse they do keep away, so no decree was needed.

bullets.text: The Gemara asks what distinguishes a *zav*, whose liquids the Sages decreed impure, from a corpse, whose liquids they did not.

Answer: since people do not naturally separate from a *zav*, the Sages added restrictions to keep others from contracting impurity from those of his liquids that are impure by Torah law; since people naturally separate from a corpse, no such decree was made.
Rashi: a *zav* or *niddah* cannot be identified by sight, while a corpse is unmistakable — so the heaviest source of impurity ends up treated more leniently in this respect than the lighter one.

Tosafot asks why the *zav*'s liquids are only rabbinically impure, since on exiting they touch his body. Two answers: the case is where the liquid was drawn off without touching the skin, or such fluids are not biblically classified as liquids at all, like a rock that cannot receive impurity.

children.title: The Two Baraitot: R. Yehuda and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
children.gist: "And he shall cover it" obligates the spurted blood and the blood on the knife, but R. Yehuda and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel each limit that obligation.

bullets.text: Baraita: "And he shall cover it" (Leviticus 17:13) teaches that one is obligated to cover blood that spurted and blood that remained on the slaughtering knife.
R. Yehuda: when is that so? When there is no blood other than that blood; but if there is other blood, one is exempt from covering it.

A second baraita: "And he shall cover it" teaches that one must cover all of the blood — from here they said that blood that spurts out and blood remaining on the sides of the animal's throat must be covered.

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: that applies only where one has not yet covered the blood of the soul, the blood that flows from the place of slaughter as the animal dies; once he covered it, he is exempt from the rest.
Rashi reads *agafayim* in the second baraita as the walls of the place of slaughter.

children.title: What "Its Blood" Means: All, Part, or the Special Blood
children.gist: The Gemara locates the three-way dispute in the word *damo*: all the blood, any part of it, or specifically the blood of the soul.

bullets.text: The Gemara asks with regard to what they disagree.
The Rabbis: "its blood" indicates an obligation to cover all of its blood, even the blood that spurts out.
R. Yehuda: "its blood" indicates that one fulfills the mitzva with any part of the blood, even a small amount of it.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: "its blood" refers to the special blood — the blood of the soul.

rows: Every drop, including spurted blood, blood on the knife and on the sides of the throat
*Afilu miktzat damo* — even part of it
Only where there is no other blood; otherwise the stray blood need not be covered
The blood of the soul; once that is covered he is exempt from the rest

children.title: Ruling: Is R. Yehuda Clarifying or Disputing?
children.gist: Because R. Yehuda opens with "when?", the Rishonim split over whether he explains the first *tanna* or argues with him, and practice tends toward the lenient readings.

bullets.text: Ordinarily one follows the *tanna kamma*, but R. Yehuda's opening word *eimatai* usually marks a clarification rather than a dispute — complicated here by the Gemara's own framing of a three-way disagreement.

Several Rishonim, including the Rambam, treat R. Yehuda as clarifying the first *tanna* and rule accordingly, and Tosafot appears to lean that way; the Ra'avad holds he dissents and rules with the Chachamim that all the blood must be covered.

In practice even a stringent ruling could not require gathering every splatter; R. Yehuda's *miktzat* means blood one cannot reach need not be pursued, not that one should deliberately do the minimum. In a slaughterhouse the main flow is covered and the knife cleaned between slaughters.

children.title: Permitted and Forbidden Substances
children.gist: Fine manure, fine sand, lime, crushed potsherd and crushed brick are valid; thick or uncrushed substances, and turning a vessel over the blood, are not.

bullets.text: Mishna: one may cover the blood with fine granulated manure, fine sand, lime, crushed potsherd, and a brick or the lid of an earthenware barrel that one crushed.
One may not cover with thick manure, with thick clumped sand, or with a brick or lid that one did not crush; neither may one merely turn a vessel over the blood.
Rashi: covering with a solid object that rests on top and can be lifted away is a different act from covering with granular material that settles in and genuinely buries the blood.

A thematic counterpoint: after Kayin's murder the blood "cries out to Me from the ground" and the earth is told not to cover it, while blood from a lawful slaughter is to be respectfully buried in the earth.

children.title: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's Principle: Plants Must Grow in It
children.gist: A general rule replaces the list: anything in which plants grow may be used, anything in which they do not may not.

bullets.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel stated a principle: a substance in which plants grow may be used to cover blood; a substance in which plants do not grow may not.

This reads as a clarification of the first *tanna* rather than a dissent, but it cannot stand alone: a thick clump of manure or earth supports growth and is still disqualified, so granularity and growth operate as two independent requirements.
A suggested reading: blood is a life-source, and the material that covers it must itself be a medium that sustains life.

children.title: Defining Fine Sand: The Potter's Standard
children.gist: R. Yochanan measures sand by whether a potter must crush it, and the two versions of his ruling part company over sand that merely crumbles by hand.

bullets.text: What is fine sand? Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of R. Yochanan: any sand that the pottery producer does not need to crush in order to use it.
Some teach the statement on the Mishna's latter clause instead: thick sand is any sand that the potter must crush in order to use it.

The practical difference is sand that requires some crushing but not full crushing — it crumbles in the hand without a tool. On the first version it may be used, since it does not require crushing; on the second version it may not, since it does require some crushing.
A recurring logical pattern: which pole of the spectrum you define determines where the ambiguous middle case lands.

sections.title: Deriving the Substances from "And Cover It With Earth"
sections.gist: A baraita expands from "and cover it" and contracts with "with earth" to reach "a type of earth in which plants grow", and the Gemara defends that method against a straightforward *klal u'prat*.

children.title: The Baraita's Expansion and Contraction
children.gist: Two lists — one included by the verb, one excluded by "with earth" — are sorted by the criterion of being a type of earth in which plants grow.

bullets.text: Baraita: one might have thought he may cover the blood with stones or merely turn a vessel over it; therefore the verse states "with earth".

From "with earth" alone I would know only earth. To include fine manure, fine sand, crushed stones, crushed potsherd, fine chaff of flax, fine sawdust of carpenters, lime, and a crushed brick or barrel lid, the verse says "and cover it" — with any substance.

One might then have included thick manure, thick sand, filings of metal vessels, an uncrushed brick or lid, flour, bran and coarse bran; therefore the verse says "and cover it with earth", showing not all substances may be used.

What determines which are included and which excluded? After the verse included with "and cover it" and excluded with "with earth", I include substances that are a type of earth in which plants grow and exclude those that are not.

Tosafot notes that the baraita's formulation — one sows in it and it sprouts — is narrower than the Mishna's "a substance in which plants grow": desert sand may host spontaneous growth but nothing sown will sprout in it, which matters for the desert case below.

children.title: Why Not Klal u'Prat? Rav Mari's Answer
children.gist: Read as a generalization and detail, the verse would permit earth alone; Rav Mari answers that this generalization needs its detail to be understood at all.

bullets.text: Objection: say that "and cover it" is the generalization and "with earth" the detail — then by the rule of *klal u'prat* only what is in the detail is included, and only earth could be used.
Rav Mari: "and cover it" is a generalization that requires its detail to clarify its nature, and such a generalization is not interpreted by the principle of *klal u'prat*.
The Gemara explains what the detail clarifies: that the blood must be covered with a substance that absorbs it, and that placing a vessel over it does not suffice.

Rashi: the verb itself is ambiguous — covering could mean laying something over, like a blanket or a vessel, or burying beneath granular material; the *prat* tells us which kind of covering is meant, so it cannot function as a limiting detail.
Tosafot reads *tzarich* differently: "with earth" was needed for another teaching — that there must be earth beneath the blood as well — so its limiting force is undermined.

One might have expected the alternative framework of *ribuy u'miut*, which yields whatever resembles the narrow term; the Gemara works within *klal u'prat* and arrives at the same operative criterion, anything similar to *afar*.

sections.gist: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's strict growth requirement is attacked by Rava and defended from a baraita about a traveler who grinds a gold coin or burns his garment.

children.title: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda vs. Rava
children.gist: Rava dismisses the requirement that seed sprout in the substance as absurd; Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak claims a baraita for it.

bullets.text: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda taught: one may cover the blood of an undomesticated animal or a bird only with a substance in which seed is sown and sprouts.
Rava: this is *burkha*, an absurdity, since the Mishna and the baraita both permit substances in which seeds do not sprout.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said to Rava: what is absurd about it? I said this statement to him, and I said it from a baraita.

children.title: The Baraita: A Gold Dinar in the Desert, a Burnt Garment at Sea
children.gist: Travelers without earth grind a gold coin or burn a garment — and the desert clause shows that sand in which seed will not sprout is disqualified.

bullets.text: Baraita: if one is traveling in the desert and has no dirt with which to cover the blood, he may grind a gold dinar into powder and cover with it.
If one is traveling on a ship and has no earth, he may burn his garment and cover the blood with the ashes.
The first clause proves the point: desert sand, in which seeds do not sprout, may not be used — the support for Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's ruling.

children.title: Ashes and Gold Dust Are Called Afar
children.gist: Ashes have a known source for being called *afar*; for gold, R. Zeira produces "dust of gold" from Job.

bullets.text: Granted the ashes, since there is a source that ashes are called *afar*, so using them accords with "and cover it with earth".
But the gold dinar — from where? R. Zeira: "And it has dust of [*afrot*] gold" (Job 28:6), showing that gold too is called dust.

Two categories of valid material thus emerge: substances that share earth's qualities (granular, growth-supporting) and substances the Torah labels *afar* even though they lack those qualities — ashes and gold dust.

sections.title: What Counts as Afar: Beit Shammai, Beit Hillel, and Later Additions
sections.gist: A baraita has Beit Shammai restricting the mitzva to earth itself while Beit Hillel admit ashes by the name *afar*, and the Sages later added further powders to the list.

children.title: Beit Shammai vs. Beit Hillel on Ashes
children.gist: Beit Hillel prove from the red heifer that ashes are called *afar*; Beit Shammai answer that they are called only "dust of the burning".

bullets.text: Baraita: one may cover the blood of an undomesticated animal or a bird only with earth — the statement of Beit Shammai.
Beit Hillel: we find that ashes are called dust, as it says of the red heifer, "they shall take from the ashes [*me'afar*] of the burning of the purification from sin" (Numbers 19:17).
Beit Shammai respond: they are called "dust of the burning", not ordinary dust.
Abraham's "and I am but dust and ashes" likewise pairs the two words, which is why the dispute turns on whether the label *afar* extends to ash on its own.

children.title: Added Substances: Coal Dust, Keḥol, Chiselings, Arsenic
children.gist: Later Sages added several fine powders to the Mishna's list, and one view even admits arsenic.

bullets.text: It is taught that the Sages added to the Mishna's list: coal dust, stibium (*keḥol*), and shavings from chiseling; and some say they included even arsenic (*zarnikh*).

Rashi identifies *shachor* as the fine powder of ground charcoal, *keḥol* as an eye salve, and the third item as the dust that accumulates in a mill; how these fit the criteria — and how a mineral like *zarnikh* is admitted when metal filings are excluded — is not fully transparent.

sections.title: Rava's Aggada: Abraham's "Dust and Ashes"
sections.gist: Rava reads two mitzvot of dust and ashes as Abraham's reward, and explains why the earth of covering the blood is not among them.

bullets.text: Rava: as reward for Abraham saying "And I am but dust and ashes" (Genesis 18:27), his children merited two mitzvot — the ashes of the red heifer and the dust of the *sota*, dirt from the ground of the Tabernacle mixed into her water.
The pairing is exact: *eifer* corresponds to the heifer's ashes, *afar* to the dust of the *sota*.
The Gemara challenges: let Rava also count the earth used for covering the blood, the subject of this whole chapter.

Answer: there the earth serves as an accessory to the mitzva but imparts no benefit — it comes after the slaughter and does not render the meat fit — whereas the heifer's ashes purify the impure and the *sota*'s dust leads to peace between husband and wife.
The paradox: one earns merit for *kissuy hadam*, yet it is not listed among the rewards precisely because it accomplishes nothing beyond the act itself.
Rava then begins a second such teaching, about Abraham's refusal of the property of the king of Sodom.

sections.continues: Continues on 89a: Rava's second teaching — Abraham's refusal of "a thread nor a shoe strap" rewarded with the *techelet* thread and the strap of *tefillin*.

judgment_calls: The plasma statements of R. Asi and R. Yirmeya (87b) are kept as their own top-level section rather than nested under the corpse-liquids challenge, since they continue the blood-mixture sugya of the previous daf; the Tosefta they lead into begins the new challenge, which starts the next section.

The shiur's material on which liquids are *avot hatumah* and on the seven liquids is attached to the mishna clause 'except for a liquid that is itself a primary source', rather than given its own section, since the Gemara text has no independent step there.

The halachic ruling on R. Yehuda (Rishonim, practice) is shiur-only and could have been folded into the dispute section; given its own child because it is a distinct question — how we rule — rather than a step in the Gemara's argument.

Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's growth requirement with the desert/ship baraita is a top-level section rather than a child of the *klal u'prat* derivation, even though both turn on the growth criterion, because the Gemara opens a new amoraic exchange there.
Beit Shammai/Beit Hillel and the added substances are grouped under one top-level heading on what counts as *afar*; each could stand alone, but the additions read as a continuation of the same list.
coverage_notes: The essay reads R. Yirmeya of Difti as 'ein bo karet' (no *karet*); the Sefaria text states that consuming the plasma is punishable by *karet*, provided there is a *kezayit* of actual blood. Followed the text, and kept the essay's analysis of the *kezayit* qualification as shiur material.

The essay says that on both versions of the potter's standard the sand that merely crumbles by hand is permitted; the text says the first version permits it and the second forbids it. Followed the text.

The exchange between Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda, Rava (*burkha*) and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak (88b.5–6) is not in the essay, which presents the desert/ship baraita directly; that subsection is outlined from the text and flagged, while the desert/ship cases and the growth criterion themselves are covered by the shiur.

The essay brings the red-heifer verse and Abraham's 'dust and ashes' as the sources for ashes being called *afar* already in the gold/ashes discussion; in the text the Gemara there only says 'we found a source', and the red-heifer verse is cited in the following Beit Hillel baraita (88b.8). Followed the text's order and placement.

The essay follows Rashi in taking *agafayim* as the walls of the slaughtering area; the Sefaria translation renders it 'the sides of the animal's throat'. Used the text's rendering in the Gemara bullet and Rashi's reading as a shiur bullet.

The essay's discussion of the bottom of 87b (blood mixed with rainwater) was largely covered at the end of the previous shiur; only the plasma statements from 87b.9–10 are included here, as 88a opens mid-exchange.
